Current protected file checks have bypass vectors:

1. **Basename matching** can be bypassed: an agent could create `/tmp/spending.ts` and modify it
2. **Regex-based bash detection** can be evaded: \`rm\$(echo '') /path\`, \`bash -c 'rm ...'\`
3. **No per-tool rate limiting**: agent can call \`corvid_send_message\` 1000x in a loop
4. **Coarse-grained permissions**: \`allowed_tools\` in DB not enforced in all contexts

**Proposed fixes:**
1. Absolute path resolution with allowlist checking against known protected directories
2. AST-based shell parser (e.g., shellparse) to detect injection patterns
3. Per-tool rate limiting (e.g., 10 \`send_message\` calls per minute per agent)
4. Enforce \`mcp_tool_permissions\` in MCP server setup; deny unlisted tools

**Files:** \`server/process/protected-paths.ts\`, \`server/mcp/sdk-tools.ts\`

If you're stuck on a boss because you're not that skilled, or maybe you have mobility issues that make the bosses too difficult, you can get people to help you and make it past those sections, if you don't know what to do next you can ask the community, but if you cannot physically see what's happening you're just not able to play the game.
Accessibility is actually really important, but the accessibility for a FromSoft game should not revolve around how it's too hard, but around how it physically limits people ability to enjoy it - and I mean physically limits people who WANT to enjoy the game, and not turn it into a completely different game because they just don't like it.

A software engineer roles is to make sure the code of the previous roles can fit the existing codebase without breaking or introducing issues.  he should be able to tell how a code could affect the whole software product. In my experience there are two things that really separate 'coders' from 'developers/engineers' that broadly align with the points in the video.

First is whether the prototype/proof-of-concept code they write ready for production. That's not to say that every edge case must be implemented, but the code should properly fit into the relevant software system or pipeline. Put another way, have they thought about how their new code will work in a real environment.

Second, do they actively revise and maintain the codebase. The adage 'If it ain't broke don't fix it' is occasionally true, but in software most often leads to technical debt. A developer/engineer will spend time revising, refactoring, documenting and testing the codebase, just as part of their daily workflow.

~~We may additionally want to ensure disclosure directly in commit messages, e.g. with "Co-authored by" clauses.~~ Up for debate. Proposed alternative: Disclosure in PR bodies.

Points of reference:

* [Fedora](https://docs.fedoraproject.org/en-US/council/policy/ai-contribution-policy/): Allowed with disclosure
* [LLVM](https://llvm.org/docs/AIToolPolicy.html): Based on the Fedora policy
* [Krita](https://krita-artists.org/t/policy-on-llm-code/178248): Outright rejection
* [Godot](https://contributing.godotengine.org/en/latest/pull_requests/pull_request_guidelines.html#doc-ai-assisted-contributions): Discouragement?
* [Linux](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/Documentation/process/coding-assistants.rst) (kernel): Allowed with disclosure.
* [NetBSD](https://www.netbsd.org/developers/commit-guidelines.html): Heavily restricted
* [Widelands](https://www.widelands.org/wiki/Contribute/): Rejection (if "purely or largely" generated)

You sent in a bug report that contains little to no information and is therefore not useful.

When you send in a report, provide all information that could be useful to us **in the first report**. Don't send in a one line report "it don't work" and expect us to ask you personally for added information, that's a waste of time and it would require you have a github account.

Just take a minute or two to provide as much information as you can, this improves the chance of getting the problem fixed a hundredfold.

Every bug report needs to contain
- Does the error happen every time or was it only once
- What are you doing (ideally with a step-by-step that triggers the issue)
- What happens (in as much detail as you can)
- What did you expect to happen

Depending on the situation these things are often useful
- log files
- screenshots (if there is anything to see)
- application state

If the bug refers to mods, always include the name of the mod, the exact version and variant and a link.

If the bug refers to a file on your system (something like "savegame can't be parsed", "ini file can't be read") - include the file in your report.

In general: use some common sense. Include whatever you think might help us find the problem. 

We usually can not fix issues that we can't see for ourselves and even when we can we can't verify if the fix works so sending a bug report that demands we just "trust you" on something doesn't make sense, whether we trust you or not doesn't matter. If we can't verify a bug exists we can't verify when it's fixed.

This is pretty interesting. I've always wondered where I would fall if I were to be categorized in the world of software development. I engineer, develop and code all the software I make, usually with the sole purpose of either solving a problem or automating something. I'm pretty lucky in the fact that I don't usually have to think too hard to see what the problem is and come up with a solution to that problem. I typically find the development part usually requires the most foresight. Not because I'm trying to solve every possible issue that may arise, but I typically try to keep things organized and extensible so that either I or someone else can make changes or add/remove functionality without breaking anything else. The coding is usually the easier part. I can code in about 8 different languages. I don't consider myself to be an expert in any language but I can read nearly any language and understand what's going on. I make frequent commits to create an easy to read audit trail. I test all of my own code, often switching between TDD and BDD (and sometimes "vibe" coding) in the same project.

The most interesting part is, although I've been creating apps/solutions/automation for nearly 30 years and I write code almost every day, I am not nor have I ever been a software developer. I'm not even in that industry. I'm a photographer. I've spent decades developing software to solve my own problems using the best possible practices even though no one else will ever read, modify or touch any of my code. It used to feel like an exercise in futility to me but I've been doing it so long now that it's just natural to me at this point.

Shifting critiques from one’s work to one’s self is something that we all do with all of our work. It takes time and typically many critiques before we move past that. I think to some degree we all believe that when we put something up for review, that we’ve also tacitly made the argument that this is what “good” code looks like. When it gets critiqued, we go from this is not good code, to I made not good code, to I look like I can’t make good code. But, your code isn’t purely a function of your competence. It’s also your time, situation, familiarity, etc. Even if it wasn’t, not producing good code now doesn’t mean that you can’t ever produce good code. It’s like this statistical irony where we know that one data point cannot define a trend until that one data point is someone critiquing our work. If you don’t believe that can happen, make once coding mistake on stream and you’ll realize so fast how quickly you can fall into that mindset 😂

I performed a controlled test to verify if this is indeed a version-specific bug or a server-side change. Using two terminals with identical setups (SuperClaude + 4 marketplace plugins) and a custom monitoring tool, I ran the exact same tasks:

v0.2.76 (Latest): Consumed ~3% of the weekly limit for the task.

v0.2.61 (Rollback): Consumed ~1% for the exact same task.

This confirms a 3:1 consumption ratio between versions. While some suggest it's purely server-side, there is definitely something in the way v2.0.76 handles context, metadata, or plugin communication that is inflating token usage significantly.

Temporary fix for those on npm: npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code@2.0.61

I used to give a test I had created for programmming applicants. The test presented a problem and a made up programming language. The test then asked what were the possible solutions, list the tradeoffs and assumptions to the solutions, pick a solution from those and implement it in the provided language. 

The applicants that skipped everything and went straight to a solution (regardless of how good the coded solutions was) - not hired, and that was the vast majority of applicants. 

We had some who attempted basically the "engineering" portion but were unable to do it. 

For those who did the solution evaluation and selection with logical choices and solutions, no matter which solution they chose to actually code, we would hire all other things being equal. We did read the code to make sure it was reasonable but the key was the problem understadning and understanding tradeoffs. 

In the years I administed the test, only one applicant had no experience in the real programming languages we were using but in the design phase stated that "Due to defects in the provided programming language, we can only code this class of solutions." One of the best hires I ever made.
